## Method

### Study design and participants

The trial was conducted online in Germany and follows a concealed, prospective, parallel group, placebo-control trial with 1:1 randomization. The study design has been prospectively published [@frombergerMyTabuAPlaceboControlled2021]. Data on re-offenses based on criminal records will be assessed in a five-year follow up. The trial was prospectively registered on April 24, 2020 in the [German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00021256)](https://drks.de/search/en/trial/DRKS00021256). The trial and development of the WBI was advised by a multidisciplinary team (a police officer, a supervision officer, and a representative of participants).
All sexual offenders under community supervision (§§56, 57, 68 StGB) from all German federal states (except Hamburg, Bremen and Saarland), which are sentenced for at least one case of CSA (§§176ff StGB) or CSEM (§184b StGB), were eligible for the trial. There exist no exclusion criteria regarding gender. Only persons who are older than 18 years were included. Exclusion criteria were a probation period shorter than 6 months at enrollment; no access to online intervention (PC, tablet or smart phone); a severe acute psychiatric disorder; a severe cerebro-organic disorder; severe cognitive impairment, (6) withdrawal of the informed consent. All participants gave written informed consent. The participants were credited with monetary compensation after completing a session if they had saved €15 (or a multiple thereof). The total amount of compensation was €120 when all sessions were completed. However, the participants were told that they would not receive any confirmation of having met the treatment requirements set by the court by taking part in the clinical trial.
Ethics approval was granted by the medical ethical board of the University Medical Center Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany, on February 21, 2020 (reference number 16/2/20).

### Randomisation and masking

The clinical trial comprises two parallel groups (intervention group and placebo group). Subjects are randomly allocated to treatment using an allocation ratio of 1:1. The randomization lists are centrally generated using a computerized system (secuTrial®, interActive Systems GmbH, Germany), stratified by the offense type (§176ff StGB vs. §184b StGB), type of community supervision, external treatment in addition to community supervison as usual, and static risk to re-offend at baseline (assessed with the modified Static-99[@setoOnlineSolicitationOffenders2012]). At screening, each subject receives the next consecutive screening number. At randomization, each subject eligible for study participation receives the next consecutive randomization number according to his stratum from a block of randomization numbers (block size: 4). Due to security reasons, blinding of supervision officers (SOs) and online coaches was not possible. Nevertheless, participants, outcome adjudicators, and data analysts (observer) have been blinded until the end of the data analysis.

### Procedures

The theoretical concept, procedures, and content of the WBI are published online [@frombergerMyTabuAPlaceboControlled2021] (see also SUPP Section "The \@myTabu framework"). The content of the intervention as well as the placebo arm are summarized in @tbl-module-content. The WBI builds on already established in-face community-based treatment programs following a cognitive-behavioral approach. Both treatment programs are designed for CSA as well as CSEM offenders [@brikenPraeventionSexuellenKindesmissbrauchs2017; @wildPreventionSexualChild2020]. The intervention arm focus solely on psychological meaningful risk factors [@setoEmpiricallybasedDynamicRisk2023]. Parts in the in-face programs adressing meaningful risk factors have been digitalized, other parts have been skipped. The WBI is designed for female as well as male participants, but due a lack of empirical evidence for specific risk factors for female individuals at WBI development, the content remains identical for women and men.

{{< include _includes/tbl_module_content.qmd >}}

The procedure was the same for both trial arms. For the recruitment of participants, scientific staff informed SOs about the clinical trial and asked them to inform individuals under their supervision. If interested, a meeting with an research assistant took place at the supervision office. During this meeting, the research assistant provided detailed information about the goals and procedure of the trial, data security and advantages or disadvantages of taking part in the trial and that he had to sign an intervention agreement. In the intervention agreement, the participant agreed not to commit offenses during the participation and is informed that any violation could lead to exclusion. After obtaining the written informed consent, the research assistant extracted data for randomization and baseline characteristics from official records on site. After allocation, the username as well as the initial password necessary to log in was delivered by post to the supervision officer, who gave it to the participant at their next regular meeting. After the first log-in, the participant had to go through an introduction section. The main WBI was divided into six modules, each module was further divided into four sessions. Participants were advised to walk through one session per week. The participants could freely decide when they will work on the session. The next session becomes unlocked, when one week has past since the last session and all guided exercises have been successfully completed. Thus, participants were able to finish each module within 4 weeks. User tests before running the trial took approximately 60 minutes to complete one session (exclusive questionnaires and working on guided exercises). In summary, the participant was able to finish the WBI within 24 weeks by investing about at least 24 hours online time.
Before and after each module, questionnaires for this module were provided automatically by the WBI online. Due to ethical reasons, before presenting the questionnaire forms for the primary outcome and the Mood and Risk Questionnaire (MRQ), participants were informed that answers will be viewable by their community supervisor. Only the SOs had access to this data during the trial. After finishing module six, the participants had access to the WBI one more week to download their individual digital first aid kit created during the WBI and to request the last expense allowance before the account was closed. To prematurely exclude a participant from the clinical trial, the supervision officer had to fill in a questionnaire on exclusion reasons (Exclusion Questionnaire, EQ) in order to request the exclusion of a participant from the trial. There was no time constraint defined at which a participant was excluded.
Due to data security aspects, the trial staff had no possibility to contact a participant during the clinical trial directly. All communication with participants took place online within the secured messanger of the WBI; communication between trial staff and community supervisors per Email, telephone or in presence. Six month before the end of the clinical trial, all remaining Ssupervision officers have been pleased to inform participants about the necessity of working as advised on the WBI in order to be able to finish it. Supervisors not logged in within one month have been automatically reminded by Email.
All participants received Community Supervision as Usual (CSaU) comprising all orders of the court and treatment as usual (e.g., in-face contacts with supervision officers, treatment ordered by court).
Study therapists (one male psychotherapist, four female psychologists) were intensively trained in the WBI by completing a practice treatment of at least one simulated participant. Regular monthly group supervisions ensured treatment consistency; the answers of online coaches on guided exercises were manualized (by predefined templates fprovided by the WBI; see SUP Figure A3)

### Outcomes

References, psychometric criteria and descriptions for all outcomes are provided in Supplementary materials "tbl-description-outcome". Primary outcomes as defined in the SAP were officially recorded re-offenses five years after last-patient-out (September 2030) and the Index of Desistance (IoD), a self-report scale [@frombergerMyTabuAPlaceboControlled2021]. The IoD was intended to measure the effectiveness of the intervention arm in reducing dynamic risk factors compared to the placebo arm. At trial start, the IoD was conceptualized as a composite measure comprising three self-report instruments developed at the outset of the research project [@nitscheErfassungAkutUnd2022]. However, recently, the items of the scales underlying the IoD have been reduced in order to enhance their psychometric quality, the CMC was removed due to low internal consistency and the scale renamed into the Child Sexual Abuse Risk Evaluation Self-Report (CARES) scale. The CARES total score is a composite measure comprising two self-report instruments. It is calculated by summing the CARES-A and CARES-S total scores, producing a range from 0 to 102, with higher scores indicating greater severity of both acute and stable dynamic risk factors [@sonjaetzlerDevelopmentInitialValidationsubmitted] (see SUPP Table XXX). Despite the deviation from the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), we report here the validated CARES scale instead of the pre-specified IoD as primary outcome (see Supplemtary material Section "IoD" for the pre-sepicified analysis). 

Secondary endpoints include specific questionnaires operationalizing the risk factors that are thematically addressed in the individual modules (see [{@tbl-risk-factors-secondary-outcomes}]). 

Re-offences are defined as the report of a hands-on offence, a hands-off offense, or a mixed offense. Re-offenses during participation in the RCT as reported by the community supervisors were derived from the Exclusion Questionnaire (EQ). The EQ assess the reasons for exclusion in a structured manner and had to be filled in by the supervisor during exclusion of a participant (see Supplementary materials "tbl-description-outcome"). Frequencies of recidivism or concrete preparations for recidivism as reported in in-app messages or during working on guided exercises have been assessed continuously (see Supplementary Material Figure A??? - act Critical event). Additionally, adverse events were assessed systematically with the Mood and Risk Questionnaire (MRQ). An adverse event was post-hoc defined as the occurence of at least one report of the highest possible subscore score. Only measures of the MRQ after each session are considered since the MRQ pre questionnaires asked explicitly on the time before the session and is thus not able to detect adverse events during working on the WBI.

Without predefined hypotheses, the Working Alliance Inventory-Short Revised (WAI-SR; see Supplementary materials "tbl-description-outcome") was used to assess therapeutic alliance with online coaches as well as with community supervisors on six timepoints, always after finishing the first session of a module. Changes in psychological well-being have been assessed with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index (WHO-5; see Supplementary materials "tbl-description-outcome"). In order to assess a possible volunteer-effect, the Questionnaire of Non-Participation (QNP; see Supplementary materials "tbl-description-outcome") was developed to assess possible reasons for not taking part in the clinical trial.

Finally, the Questionnaire for Acceptance of Technology (ATQ) and the Questionnaire of Subjective Therapy Preconditions (SBV-R; see Supplementary materials "tbl-description-outcome") were administered. Results of these questionnaires are not related to the hypotheses. Partly, preliminary data from the intermediate analysis has already been published with regard to the ATQ [@schroderAcceptanceWebBasedIntervention2024; @schroderEngagementWebbasedIntervention2025].

### Statistical analysis

A priori, a rate of 50% of screened participants taking voluntarily part in the clinical trial was assumed. Based on the estimation of responsible ministries of two federal states, it was expected to see 1.165 subjects eligible for participation during the recruitment period of which 50% (n = 582) have been expected to participate in the study. Taking a dropout of 26.4% into account, it was expected to see n = 428 subjects completing the HBI. With n = 214 subjects in both conditions it is possible to detect small effects (d = 0.27) with a power of 80% at a significance level α = 5%.

The statistical analysis plan was signed off before final database lock and unmasking. Data analysis was performed using the software R, version 4.5.0 [@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2025]. Interim analysis has been done by a independent data safety monitoring board (DSMB) on April 20, 2022. Stopping guideline have been prospectively desfined: The clinical trial would have been stopped if an interim analysis at 12 months after first patient in (tested on subjects having completed at least two modules of the web-based intervention) demonstrates: (a) a significantly higher risk to re-offend (based on main outcome and number of reported significant events in the experimental condition compared to the placebo condition); (b) a significantly higher proportion of reported significant events (see a) in the experimental condition than in the placebo condition; (c) a significantly increased proportion of high-risk subjects (defined in terms of the main outcome) compared to the proportion at baseline.

Statistical analyses for the primary outcome was performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. The ITT population was defined as all participants who have completed at least one module but not necessarily answered the questionnaires at the end of module one. The primary outcome (CARES total score) was analyzed by means of Gaussian linear model for repeated measures (MMRM) with treatment group, time (six time-points; after each online intervention module), treatment-by-time interaction, and the randomization strata as factors (offense type, type of CS, external treatment in addition to CSaU), baseline measurements (at clearing up) of the outcome and potentially time span from baseline as covariate and the classical IoD as dependent variable. The error terms were assumed to follow a multivariate normal distribution with unstructured covariance. Least squares mean changes from baseline are reported for the treatment groups with 95% confidence interval (CI) as well as the difference between the least squares treatment group means with 95% CI and p-value testing the null hypothesis of no treatment effect. A sensitivity analysis on imputed values complemented the analysis. Imputation has been done using multiple reference based imputation followed by ANCOVA models [@wolbersStandardReferencebasedConditional2022]. Exploratory, non-parametric Brunner-Munzel test [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000] for paired data was used to compare the pre- and post-module scores within each trial arm (adjusting the p-values using the Bonferroni-Holm’s method to control the family-wise error rate). Additionally, differences (post - pre) from baseline have been compared exploratively between the treatment groups using the Brunner-Munzel test for unpaired data [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000]. If discontinuation from study was due to clear evidence for recidivism or concrete preparation for or intention to recidivism (assessed by responsible supervision officer or online coach) the subject receives the maximal value for IoD for the remaining measurements (assuming the worst case of a failed treatment).

To analyze the treatment effects of each individual module, secondary endpoints have been analyzed using the non-parametric Brunner-Munzel test [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000] for paired data comparing the pre- and post-module scores within each trial arm and adjusting the p-values using the Bonferroni-Holm’s method to control the family-wise error rate. Additionally, differences (post - pre) from baseline have been compared exploratively between the treatment groups using the Brunner-Munzel test for unpaired data [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000]. The effect of each module on the scores corresponding to the secondary endpoints was further exploratory analyzed by fitting linear models with treatment group and the randomization strata as factors (offense type, type of CS, external treatment in addition to CSaU), pre module scores as covariate and post module scores as dependent variable if appropriate. If necessary, the scores have been transformed before the analysis. If the assumptions of a linear model were not fulfilled either an ordinal regression model was fitted analogously instead or the score was dichotomized in order to fit a logistic regression model analogously. Analyses on the secondary endpoints were carried out on the specific per-protocol (PP) population. The PP population for a specific module consists of all participants who have completed this module and provided pre- and post module data.

Frequencies and percentages of occurrences of re-offences during the clinical trial as assessed by the supervision officers are reported and differences between arms on each subscale were compared using Fisher’s exact tests and adjusting the p-values using the Bonferroni-Holm’s method to control the family-wise error rate. Frequencies and percentages of participants reporting at least one adverse event during working on the WBI are rprovided for each single-item subscales of the MRQ and differences between arms on each subscale were compared using Fisher’s exact tests and adjusting the p-values using the Bonferroni-Holm’s method to control the family-wise error rate. 

Ancilliary outcomes have been analyzed post-hoc in a exploratory manner. The total score of the WHO-5 was analyzed by means of MMRM with treatment group, time (six time-points), treatment-by-time interaction, and the randomization strata as factors (offense type, type of CS, external treatment in addition to CSaU), baseline measurements (at clearing up) of the outcome and potentially time span from baseline as covariate and the WHO-5 total score as dependent variable. The error terms were assumed to follow a multivariate normal distribution with unstructured covariance. Least squares mean changes from baseline are reported for the treatment groups with 95% confidence interval (CI) as well as the difference between the least squares treatment group means with 95% CI and p-value testing the null hypothesis of no treatment effect. The same analysis rationale was applied for the WAI-SR COACH and WAI-SR SUPERVISOR.

### Role of funding source

The work was funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (Funding number: 01KR1807A). The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report.
